# Compatible common simplex envelopes: attainment and exact contact balance

All volumes here are ordinary d-dimensional Lebesgue volumes. There is
no mixed-integer depth assertion in this note. A simplex orientation
means the d+1 outward facet directions of a full-dimensional bounded
simplex, with arbitrary positive scalings of those normals. For each
nonempty compact convex set A in R^d and such an orientation U, define

    P_U(A)={x:u_j.x<=h_A(u_j), j=0,...,d},        (1)
    h_A(u)=max_(x in A) u.x.

If A has more than one point, P_U(A) is a full-dimensional simplex.
If A is a singleton, P_U(A)=A. Indeed, after an invertible linear
map sending the facet directions to those of the standard simplex
T, (1) is

    P_U(A)=a+rT,
    a_k=min_(x in A) x_k,
    r=max_(x in A) sum_k x_k-sum_k a_k>=0.        (2)

Equality r=0 forces every x in A to have x_k=a_k for all k.
Thus only a singleton has zero radius. All nonzero-radius envelopes
for one U are positive homothets of one another.

## 1. All actual sampled convex inclusions are preserved

Let I be a finite index set of bases z in R^n and let A_z be nonempty
compact convex sets in R^d. Assume the sampled Minkowski inclusions

    sum_(i=1)^k theta_i A_(z_i) subset A_z
    whenever theta_i>=0, sum_i theta_i=1,
              sum_i theta_i z_i=z in I.         (3)

Actual fibers A_z={x:(z,x) in C} of a convex set C satisfy (3),
by applying convexity to one point chosen independently from each
fiber. For every common simplex orientation U the envelopes satisfy
the same inclusions:

    sum_i theta_i P_U(A_(z_i)) subset P_U(A_z).  (4)

To prove this, support functions in (3) give

    sum_i theta_i h_(A_(z_i))(u_j)<=h_(A_z)(u_j)

for each j. Parallel simplex addition in (2) shows that the sum
on the left of (4) is exactly the simplex, possibly a singleton,
with these summed facet offsets. It therefore obeys every inequality
defining the right side of (4).

Consequently the compact convex hull

    C_U=conv union_(z in I) ({z} times P_U(A_z))

has fiber exactly P_U(A_z) at every z in I. One inclusion comes
from the generators. For the other, write a point of the convex
hull as a finite convex combination of generator points, group
the terms with the same base, and apply (4). If I is the set of
all nonempty integer fibers of a bounded convex body C, then
conv(I) subset proj_(R^n) C. Every integer base in conv(I) therefore
belongs to I. Thus C_U has exactly the prescribed integer fibers
and no additional integer base outside I. This statement does not
assert that C_U has interior in R^(n+d): the integer bases may
lie in a lower-dimensional affine subspace.

## 2. An attained optimum among all common orientations

Take full-dimensional compact convex bodies A_1,...,A_N in R^d
and strictly positive weights w_1,...,w_N. Then the finite objective

    F(U)=sum_i w_i |P_U(A_i)|                    (5)

attains its minimum over all simplex orientations U. The proof below
also gives the extension to nonempty compact convex members provided
at least one positive-weight member is full dimensional; the possible
zero-radius envelopes and d=1 endpoint are treated explicitly.

The assumption of a full-dimensional member is material. For a
single nontrivial segment in R^2, enclosing triangles have areas
arbitrarily close to zero, while every triangle P_U(A) has positive
area by (2). Thus the infimum is not attained in that example.
Zero-weight members, if present in a larger collection, can be
omitted from (5); a full-dimensional member must have positive weight
for the argument below. Singleton members have zero cost and no
effect on the optimization.

### Proof with an explicit bound preventing escaping vertices

Choose a full-dimensional member A_*, of weight w_*, and an interior
ball B(x_*,rho) subset A_* with rho>0. A fixed initial orientation
has finite objective M. In a minimizing sequence we may discard
initial terms and assume F(U_l)<=M. Its anchor simplex

    S_l=P_(U_l)(A_*)

contains A_* and has volume at most M/w_*. Each vertex v of S_l
satisfies

    |v-x_*| <= dM/[w_* kappa_(d-1) rho^(d-1)],  (6)

where kappa_(d-1) is the volume of the unit (d-1)-ball and
kappa_0=1. The cone from the equatorial (d-1)-disk of the interior
ball, perpendicular to v-x_*, to v is contained in S_l and has
volume kappa_(d-1)rho^(d-1)|v-x_*|/d. Comparing with M/w_*
proves (6).

In the main case of all full-dimensional members, choose an interior
ball B(x_i,rho_i) in each A_i. The very same cone argument gives,
for EVERY vertex v of P_(U_l)(A_i),

    |v-x_i| <=dM/[w_i kappa_(d-1) rho_i^(d-1)]. (6a)

Thus each positive-weight fiber's simplex is individually bounded,
not merely the anchor simplex.

Label each simplex's d+1 vertices arbitrarily. A subsequence gives
simultaneous limits v_0,...,v_d. Their hull S is the Hausdorff limit
of S_l and contains A_*, so it is full dimensional. Thus these
d+1 limiting vertices are affinely independent, and S is a simplex.
Its corresponding facet normals and offsets can be chosen to vary
continuously with the vertices, for example as outward unit normals.
To see this directly, each facet normal is the normalized null vector
of its d-1 independent edge differences, with sign determined by the
opposite vertex; affine independence keeps the denominator and sign
strict. For d=1 the two outward unit normals are constant after the
endpoint labeling.

Write u_(j,l) for these outward unit normals and u_j for their
limits. Every facet of S_l supports A_* by construction, so its
offset is h_(A_*)(u_(j,l)). Support functions of fixed compact sets
are continuous, as

    |h_A(u)-h_A(v)|<=max_(x in A)|x| |u-v|.

It follows that S=P_U(A_*) for the limiting orientation U.

For every other fixed A_i, the numbers h_(A_i)(u_(j,l)) converge
to h_(A_i)(u_j). Each candidate vertex of P_(U_l)(A_i) is the
intersection of d of these d+1 planes. The corresponding matrices
are nonsingular at the limiting orientation, so their inverses
and the intersection points converge. Formula (2) shows that these
are the actual vertices of the enclosing simplex; if A_i is a
singleton, all the points coincide, which is harmless. Determinant
continuity gives

    |P_(U_l)(A_i)| -> |P_U(A_i)|.

There are only finitely many terms in (5), hence F(U_l)->F(U).
The limiting U attains the infimum. This proves existence without
assuming a compact space of all orientations or ignoring potential
degeneration of its simplices.

The homothety parameters can also be tracked explicitly. Relative
to the anchor write P_(U_l)(A_i)=a_(i,l)+r_(i,l) S_l. For a full
dimensional A_i,

    (w_*|A_i|/M)^(1/d) <= r_(i,l)
                     <=(M/(w_i|A_*|))^(1/d).   (6b)

These inequalities follow from r_(i,l)^d=|P_(U_l)(A_i)|/|S_l|,
the containing-body lower volume bounds, and the objective upper
bounds. The vertex convergence already proved makes these ratios
converge. Their translations are
a_(i,l)=g(P_(U_l)(A_i))-r_(i,l)g(S_l), where g denotes the vertex
centroid of a simplex, and therefore converge as well. For a
singleton member the ratio is exactly zero and its translation
is its fixed point. For other lower-dimensional members in the
extension, the limiting radius is positive by (2); continuity of
the vertex systems supplies boundedness without an interior-ball
bound for that member.

## 3. A one-facet directional derivative without smoothness assumptions

For a compact convex set A, a nonzero vector u, and any vector v,
put F_A(u)={x in A:u.x=h_A(u)}. Then the right derivative is

    (d/dt)_(t=0+) h_A(u+tv)=h_(F_A(u))(v).       (7)

Indeed every maximizer in F_A(u) gives the corresponding lower
bound on the difference quotient. For an upper bound choose a
maximizer x_t for u+tv. The quotient is at most v.x_t, because
u.x_t<=h_A(u). Every convergent subsequence of x_t as t decreases
to zero has limit in F_A(u), by compactness and continuity. This
proves the upper bound and (7), including exposed faces of positive
dimension and nondifferentiable support functions.

Consider now one full-dimensional simplex P, with a selected facet
F={x in P:u.x=h}, whose opposite vertex is q. Keep the other d
facet planes fixed, change u to u+tv, and change the selected
offset to h(t)=h+t k+o(t). Let p_1,...,p_d be the vertices of F
and L=h-u.q>0. The moving selected vertices are exactly

    p_l(t)=q+s_l(t)(p_l-q),
    s_l(t)=[h(t)-(u+tv).q]/[(u+tv).(p_l-q)]
           =1+t[k-v.p_l]/L+o(t).               (8)

For small t the coefficients are positive and the combinatorics
are unchanged. The determinant formula therefore gives

    |P(t)|=|P| product_(l=1)^d s_l(t),
    (d/dt)_(0+) |P(t)|
       = (H_(d-1)(F)/|u|)[k-v.c_F],            (9)

where c_F=(p_1+...+p_d)/d. The equality uses
|P|=H_(d-1)(F)L/(d|u|). Thus (9) follows from a finite determinant,
without a differentiability assumption on A or an unproved shape
derivative formula.

If P=P_U(A) and the selected facet normal alone is changed,
its offset changes to h_A(u+tv). Substituting (7) into (9) yields

    (d/dt)_(0+) |P_(U(t))(A)|
      = (H_(d-1)(F)/|u|)
                 [h_(F_A(u))(v)-v.c_F].        (10)

For a singleton A, its envelope is the same singleton under every
orientation; its volume derivative is zero.

## 4. Exact necessary first-order aggregate contact conditions

Assume d>=2 and first take all the bodies in (5) to be full
dimensional. Let U minimize (5). Choose a fixed representative
simplex T having orientation U and write

    P_U(A_i)=a_i+r_i T,

with r_i>0 for every member. For each facet j let
c_(ij) be the centroid of the corresponding envelope facet and

    F_(ij)={x in A_i:u_j.x=h_(A_i)(u_j)}.

Then, for every j, the following exact membership holds:

    sum_i w_i r_i^(d-1) c_(ij)
                  in sum_i w_i r_i^(d-1) F_(ij). (11)

The right side is a Minkowski sum with scalar coefficients.
Equivalently there exist actual points x_(ij) in F_(ij) such that

    sum_i w_i r_i^(d-1)(x_(ij)-c_(ij))=0.        (12)

### Proof and scope of stationarity

Changing just u_j to u_j+tv preserves a simplex orientation for
all sufficiently small |t|. One elementary verification is to
keep the other d normals fixed, whose planes at fixed offsets
meet at one point: the selected intercepts along the d opposite
edge rays remain positive under a small perturbation, and hence
still define a bounded full-dimensional simplex. Equivalently,
positive spanning by d+1 normals and independence of every d
normals are open conditions. Every nonsingleton envelope remains
full dimensional by (2).

The corresponding facet areas are
r_i^(d-1) H_(d-1)(F_j(T)). Equations (10) and (5) show that the
right derivative is exactly

    F'(U; j,v)
      = [H_(d-1)(F_j(T))/|u_j|]
          sum_i w_i r_i^(d-1)
                      [h_(F_(ij))(v)-v.c_(ij)]. (13)

The factor in square brackets is strictly positive. At a minimizer
(13) is nonnegative for every v. The support function of the compact convex Minkowski
sum on the right of (11) is the sum of these weighted support
functions. The characterization of membership by all support
inequalities, or strict separation of a point outside a compact
convex set, makes (13) equivalent to (11). Membership in the finite
Minkowski sum is exactly the existence assertion (12).

For completeness these are precisely the conditions for all first
directional derivatives under simultaneous linear changes of the
facet normals to be nonnegative. The volume of a nondegenerate
simplex is a smooth function of its facet normals and offsets in
a neighborhood with fixed labels: solve its d-by-d vertex systems
and take the determinant with its constant local sign. Offsets
have the right expansions (7), so the full right derivative is
the sum of the one-facet derivatives (10). If (11) holds for every
j, each summand is nonnegative. Conversely one-facet variations
are among these simultaneous variations and force (11).

This is only FIRST-ORDER stationarity. It is not a sufficient
condition for a local or global minimum of the nonlinear objective
(5). In d=1, envelopes are the original intervals or points,
so the objective is independent of the only possible orientation;
there is no need to interpret a zero radius to the zeroth power.

The same proof extends (11)-(13) to the lower-dimensional members
permitted in Section 2. A nonsingleton member still has positive
radius by (2), so its envelope and its derivative obey precisely
the displayed formulas. For a singleton, set r_i=0 and c_(ij)
equal to its point. Its contribution to the objective is constantly
zero, and the coefficient r_i^(d-1) is zero since d>=2. Thus its
contribution on both sides of (11) and in (13) is zero. This treats
all zero-radius and dimensional cases in that extension explicitly.

There is a geometric restatement that records exactly what this
condition provides. Put b_i=w_i r_i^(d-1) for d>=2 and form

    B=sum_i b_i A_i,       P=sum_i b_i P_U(A_i).

The latter is a full-dimensional simplex and its j-th facet centroid
is sum_i b_i c_(ij), by addition of parallel simplices. Equation
(11) puts this centroid in B on its supporting j-th facet plane.
Thus every facet centroid of P belongs to B. This does not assert
that P is a minimum enclosing simplex of B. If the A_i came from
integer bases z_i, the normalized coefficients b_i/sum_k b_k
would generally have a NONINTEGER mean base. Neither (11) nor (12)
places their associated point in a required mixed-integer fiber.
Nor does (11) imply c_(ij) belongs to A_i for any individual i:
only the weighted sum of contact displacements is constrained.

## 5. The gap that compatibility alone does not remove

Attainment makes a simple obstruction rigorous. In dimension d>=2
take two full-dimensional simplices A and B that are not translates
of positive homothets of one another. Their common-orientation
minimum has strictly positive excess over |A|+|B| (weights 1,1).
For otherwise an attaining U would have

    |P_U(A)|+|P_U(B)|=|A|+|B|.

Each term on the left is at least its corresponding term on the
right. Equality of volume for nested full-dimensional compact convex
bodies forces equality of the bodies. Hence A=P_U(A) and B=P_U(B),
which would make A and B translated positive homothets, a contradiction.

This is an actual sampled-fiber example: put A at base 0 and B at
base 1 in R times R^d and take their convex hull. It is a convex
body and has precisely those two nonempty integer fibers. Each
individual ordinary depth deficit from Gamma_d is zero, yet the
minimum common-orientation volume excess is positive. All the sampled
inclusions (3) hold. Therefore no bound of this common-orientation
excess by a constant times the sum of individual ordinary depth
deficits can hold in general. Additional midpoint hypotheses or
mass restrictions would need a separate proved argument; none is
assumed in this note.

## 6. Exact stationary family with no individual centroid contacts

The aggregate condition cannot be strengthened to individual contacts,
and it is not sufficient for optimality. Both points can be seen in
one exact two-triangle example. In R^2 let T=conv(0,e_1,e_2), and
put, with equal weights,

    A=conv((3/5,2/5),(0,3/5),(2/5,0)),
    B=conv((2/5,3/5),(0,2/5),(3/5,0)).

Both standard-orientation envelopes are T. Each triangle meets each
facet of T at a single one of its displayed vertices. On the top
facet these contact points sum to (1,1), on the left facet they
sum to (0,1), and on the bottom facet they sum to (1,0). These
are exactly twice the three facet centroids of T. Since both
envelope radii are 1, (11) holds at every facet; indeed every first
directional derivative in (13) is zero. Each individual contact
point differs from the associated facet centroid, so none of the
individual facet-centroid contacts follows from (11).

The total cost for this stationary orientation is 1. It is not
minimal. Use instead the orientation of A, whose outward normals
may be chosen as

    (1,3), (-3,-2), (2,-1).

Its support offsets for A are respectively 9/5,-6/5,4/5, and for
B they are 11/5,-4/5,6/5, by direct maximization on the displayed
vertices. Hence in this orientation

    P(A)=A,
    P(B)=(-2/7,-2/7)+(13/7)A.

The determinant formula gives |A|=7/50. The new total cost is

    (7/50)[1+(13/7)^2]=109/175<1.               (14)

Thus a full set of exact aggregate facet contact balances does not
even certify the global optimum of the common-orientation problem.
Placing these A and B at integer bases 0 and 1 again realizes an
actual convex two-fiber family. The counterexample concerns the
proposed stronger stationarity interpretations, not (OC).
